decisions.0: Ace-three offsuit calls the small blind's open: the price is good and you have position for the rest of the hand. An ace is strong against the small blind's wide range, so it also 3-bets some of the time.
decisions.1: Top pair with a three kicker is ahead of most of the small blind's bets, but any better ace beats it. Calling keeps the pot small and keeps bluffs and weaker pairs in; raising mostly folds those and gets called by better aces. So calling is the natural play and raising is only a tiny bit worse. Folding would be a big mistake.
decisions.2: The ten lets nine-eight make a straight, and your three kicker no longer plays, so your top pair is now a medium-strength hand. After the small blind checks, checking behind keeps the pot small and reaches the river cheaply; a big bet would fold the weaker hands and get called by better aces and straights. Checking is better by a small margin.
decisions.3: The small blind bets half the pot on a river that changed nothing. Its bets here include many tens and missed draws, which your pair of aces beats; you need to win 25% and you win about 81%, so call. Going all-in is a big mistake: the weaker hands fold and only better hands call, which costs 9.41 bb.

takeaway: With a weak kicker, keep the pot small: call bets and check when checked to, rather than raise hands that only better hands will call.
